title: Heal Her Now: Moses' Prayer for Miriam
carry: a short, true prayer is real prayer
tomorrow: why does Psalm 1 call the Torah "his" halfway through?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a question left open, and the Talmud's word for it: teiku, let it stand. Unsure is honest. And still, people pray.

The texts that matter most are often the shortest: here. ok. on my way. In the Torah, Miriam stands outside the camp, her skin suddenly white as snow. Aaron turns to his brother and begs him to do something. Moses has spent whole chapters speaking with God. This time, he says one line.
screen: `HERE. OK. ON MY WAY.` → `MIRIAM, OUTSIDE THE CAMP.` → `ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: "And Moses cried unto the LORD, saying: 'Heal her now, O God, I beseech Thee.'" In Hebrew it's El na refa na lah. No titles, no speech, no list of reasons. A brother, scared for his sister. The Talmud holds this up when it talks about prayer: a prayer can be long, and it can be this short. Then the story keeps going. God answers that Miriam will be shut out of the camp for seven days. And the people don't move on without her. The whole camp waits until she's brought back in. So the prayer that becomes yours might be long and fixed, from the siddur: the Shema in the morning, the Amidah at a service. It might be a psalm line you know by heart. It might be one short, true sentence in a hospital hallway, the way Moses said his. Both are prayer in this tradition. Something to tell a friend tonight: Moses' prayer for his sister fits in a single breath.

segments.voice: Say the prayer that's become yours, out loud and slowly: a line from the siddur, a psalm, or the short words you actually reach for. If you don't pray, say one sentence you'd want someone to say for a person you love.

howItsDone: Jewish prayer includes the fixed services of the siddur, said daily, and personal prayer in a person's own words; Moses' short prayer for Miriam is often cited as a model of a brief, heartfelt prayer.
